newsitem.title: UK: Deutsche admits failings over fund controls - FT.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche admits failings over fund controls - FT.

text.p: Germany's mighty Deutsche Bank has admitted to a breakdown of controls and supervision in its British-based fund management arm Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), the Financial Times said on Friday.

The paper reported that Michael Dobson, chief executive of Deutsche's investment banking arm Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said a City law firm and an accountancy firm would be involved in an internal inquiry into what had happened at MGAM.

"There is a clear structure and there was a breakdown of controls and supervision. We will leave no stone unturned to discover what happened and make sure it never happens again," the paper reported Dobson, a Deutsche Bank director, as saying.
It said Deutsche considered moving the British unit trust business under Frankfurt's control and would do so again in light of apparent irregularities in three of the funds.

On Thursday Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) was drawn closer to the probe. It also emerged the investigation had cast its net overseas, as City regulatory sources confirmed newspaper reports that the inquiry extended beyond Britain.

British papers said a number of holding companies listed in Luxembourg were under the microscope of investigators as the role of investments in European technology stocks which breached City rules came under close scrutiny.
A spokeswoman for the SFO said it was in contact with investment watchdog Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO), which would share any relevant material.
The Times said overseas authorities, in the United States, Luxembourg and Switzerland, had also become involved.
After the 1.4 billion stg funds, which were suspended on Monday, resumed trading, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said nearly eight percent, or around 100 million stg, had been redeemed.
The funds resumed trading after Deutsche spent 180 million stg ($282.4 million) removing certain unlisted securities.
"This is good news because people were predicting they would be selling lots...but there has been no panic selling," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell spokesman James Murray.
But industry sources said this level of redemptions in a day was a major reverse.
IMRO's own probe into MGAM has already led to the suspension of two fund managers and briefly saw trading halted in three MGAM funds, which have around 90,000 small investors.
